title: Checkpoint: A Building Is Designed in the Order Its Decisions Become Irreversible
summary: This checkpoint lesson pulls the design phase into one idea: every design decision has a last responsible moment, after which changing it costs money, time or safety. Learn which decisions lock first, who owns each one, and how the stage gate protects you from discovering the mistake on site.
body:
Designing a building is not drawing a picture and then filling it in. It is a chain of decisions, each one closing options for the next, and the owner's job is to make the expensive, irreversible ones first, on purpose, with the right person signing for each.

Recall

Q. What is life-cycle cost?

A. The total cost of owning a building element over its life: first cost, plus energy, maintenance, repair and replacement, brought back to today's money. A cheap roof that must be replaced twice can cost more than an expensive one replaced never.

Q. What is the difference between legally required standby power and optional standby power?

A. Legally required standby serves loads a code or authority demands, such as certain smoke control or sewage pumps, while optional standby serves loads the owner chooses to protect, such as refrigeration or a business system. The National Electrical Code treats them as separate systems with different rules.

Q. Why does the occupancy classification matter so much at the start of a design?

A. Because the occupancy, for example transient lodging versus permanent residential, drives the construction type, the allowable height and area, the fire protection and the egress, so getting it wrong ripples through every other discipline.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, this is the checkpoint for the phase on designing the building. Over ten weeks you met the brief, resilience, the code basis, egress, fire, structure, envelope, building services and life-cycle cost. Each was taught in its own week by its own specialist. On a real project they arrive at the same time, on the same drawings, and they fight each other for the same space and the same dollars. The developer who wins is not the one who knows the most code. It is the one who knows which decisions lock first and refuses to let them drift.

The last responsible moment

In plain English: every decision has a date after which changing it gets expensive. Before that date a change is a sketch. After it, a change is a redesign, a re-permit or a demolition.

The professional term is the last responsible moment: the latest point at which a decision can be made without closing off a better option or forcing rework. Design management is the discipline of listing those moments and making each decision just before it, with the evidence in hand. Too early and you decide on guesses. Too late and the decision is made for you by whatever has already been drawn.

Here is the rough order in which the big decisions lock, for a hypothetical mid-rise mixed-use building. First, the use and occupancy, because they set the code path. Second, the construction type and the height and area strategy, because they set the structural material and the fire protection. Third, the flood and wind basis, because they set the ground floor level and the glazing. Fourth, the structural grid and floor-to-floor height, because every service must fit inside them. Fifth, the location of stairs, shafts and risers, because they cannot move once the slabs are poured. Envelope details, finishes and most equipment choices come later, and can stay flexible longer.

Worked example. Suppose the team is in schematic design and the operator asks to convert two floors from apartments to short-stay suites. If that change is raised before the code analysis is fixed, the cost is a few weeks of consultant time, say a hypothetical 40,000 dollars. If it is raised after the structure is detailed and the permit is filed, the occupancy change may alter sprinkler design, corridor ratings, travel distances and possibly the construction type. The same change can now cost a hypothetical 800,000 dollars and four months. The request did not change. The date did.

Say that out loud now.

One owner for every interface

The second idea of the phase is that most design failures happen between disciplines, not inside them. The structural engineer designs a sound slab. The mechanical engineer designs a sound duct. Nobody owns the hole the duct needs through the slab, the fire rating of that hole, or the beam that was moved to make room for it.

The professional tool is a responsibility matrix, a table that lists every interface and names one consultant responsible for coordinating it. Typical interfaces: slab penetrations and firestopping, the envelope at the structural frame, equipment loads on the roof, flood barriers at doors, and smoke control against the mechanical system. Building information modelling, or BIM, a shared three-dimensional digital model of the building, helps by detecting clashes, places where two elements occupy the same space. But a clash report only finds geometry. It does not find a fire rating that was assumed and never designed. That needs a named person.

Worked example. A hypothetical project has 30 shafts and 400 slab penetrations. If each penetration has a one percent chance of being missed in coordination, you would expect about 4 problems. Found in the model, each costs perhaps 500 dollars to fix. Found on site after the slab is poured, each costs perhaps 15,000 dollars in coring, structural checks and delay. That is roughly 2,000 dollars against 60,000 dollars for the same four mistakes.

How the best do it

The strongest design teams run formal stage gates: at the end of each design stage, the design is frozen, an independent reviewer who did not draw it checks it against the brief, the code basis and the cost plan, and the owner signs a decision to proceed. Large firms often keep a design review panel of senior staff from outside the project for exactly this purpose. A small developer can copy the habit cheaply: a written brief, a one-page gate checklist, one paid outside review at the end of schematic design and at the end of design development, and a signed decision log.

Six-Lens Check

Tax: design decisions shape how costs are classified between building, equipment and land improvements, which can affect depreciation; ask a tax adviser before the cost plan is fixed. Liability: every consultant's scope and professional liability insurance should match the interfaces they own. Banking: the lender will want to see the design frozen and costed before it commits. Governance: the decision log records who approved each locked decision. Estate: design records are part of the asset an heir or trustee inherits. Exit: a buyer will ask for the code analysis, the structural calculations and the commissioning records.

Professional sign-off required: architect of record, for the code analysis and coordination; structural engineer of record, for the frame and every opening through it.

Long-lead decisions hide inside the design

A second kind of lock is procurement. Some equipment, such as elevators, switchgear, generators and specialist glazing, can take many months to manufacture. If the design leaves those choices open until bidding, the delivery date, not the design, sets the opening date. So the design manager pulls those decisions forward: the elevator count and speed, the electrical service size and the facade system are fixed early enough for the contractor to order them on award. This is the same idea as the last responsible moment, seen from the supplier's side.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is a late change to use, load or layout that every discipline hears about at a different time. The control is a change procedure that stops the design, routes the change to every consultant, prices it and reaches a signed owner decision before anyone draws it.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner treats the design as flexible until construction because drawings look easy to change. They are, until they are not. Ask your architect for a list of decisions with their last responsible moments, and put the dates in your schedule.

Callback

In Week 48, Marco taught the owner's decision log. This phase shows why it matters. A design is the accumulation of decisions, and if you cannot say who decided the occupancy, the floor height or the flood level, and when, you cannot defend the building to a lender, an authority or a buyer.

Recap

Design decisions lock in order: use, construction type, flood and wind basis, structure and floor height, then shafts and stairs. Make each just before its last responsible moment. Name one owner for every interface, and use stage gates with an independent review to catch what each discipline misses alone.

Next: Ford on Failure Forensics: the Sampoong Department Store collapse of 1995.
checklist: I have a written brief that fixes use, occupancy and quality level.
I have a list of the major design decisions with their last responsible moments.
I have a responsibility matrix naming one consultant for each interface.
I hold a stage gate with an independent review at the end of each design stage.
I route every change of use, load or layout through a priced, signed change procedure.
I keep a decision log showing who approved each locked decision and when.
I know which design records a lender, authority and buyer will ask for.
head: Field checklist
speak: Designing a building is a chain of decisions, and each one closes options for the next. The big ones lock in order: the use and occupancy, the construction type and height strategy, the flood and wind basis, the structural grid and floor height, then the stairs and shafts. Every decision has a last responsible moment, the latest point you can decide without forcing rework. Before it, a change is a sketch. After it, the same change can cost twenty times as much. Most design failures happen between disciplines, at the slab penetration nobody owned or the fire rating nobody designed. So I name one consultant for every interface, I hold a stage gate at the end of each design stage with an independent reviewer, and I route every change through a priced, signed procedure. My decision log records who decided what and when, because that is what I will be asked to prove.
terms: Last responsible moment — the latest point a decision can be made without closing off a better option or forcing rework.
Responsibility matrix — a table that names one party responsible for coordinating each design interface.
Stage gate — a formal pause at the end of a design stage where the design is frozen, reviewed and approved before the next stage begins.

hostile.q: Your design is only at schematic stage. Why should I believe your cost plan will hold?
hostile.a: Because the decisions that drive most of the cost are already locked and recorded: occupancy, construction type, flood level, structural grid and floor height. The cost plan is priced against those, with a design contingency sized for the stage we are at. At the end of design development an independent reviewer will check the design against the brief and the cost plan before I commit, and I will share that report with you.

title: Sampoong 1995: The Building That Became Something Else
summary: In 1995 the Sampoong Department Store in Seoul collapsed, killing more than 500 people. The building had been redesigned during construction for a heavier, different use, and warning cracks were seen but the building was not evacuated. Ford takes it through seven steps and draws one rule about changes of use.
body:
Sampoong did not fall because one engineer made one error. It fell because a building designed for one purpose was changed, piece by piece, into another, and each change was approved by people who did not own the structure.

Recall

Q. What is a stage gate in design management?

A. A formal pause at the end of a design stage where the design is frozen, independently reviewed and approved by the owner before work continues.

Q. What is crime prevention through environmental design, or CPTED?

A. An approach that reduces crime through the design of the place itself: natural surveillance, clear territory, controlled access and maintenance, so that security is built into layout and lighting rather than added later.

Q. What is construction type in the building code?

A. A classification of the building's structural and fire-resisting materials, from noncombustible to combustible, that sets how tall and how large the building may be for its occupancy.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, the checkpoint for the design phase needs a failure that crosses every discipline at once. Sampoong does. It is a case about change of use, structural margin, roof loads, ignored warnings and the moment when money outranked life. Every one of those can happen on a small project. The facts below are the broad, well-documented outline; read the official accounts for detail before you quote them.

Step 1: Timeline

The Sampoong building in Seoul, South Korea, was planned in the late 1980s, reportedly first as an office building, and was converted during construction into a department store. It opened in 1990. On 29 June 1995, after hours of visible cracking that day, the store collapsed in seconds while full of shoppers and staff. More than 500 people died and many hundreds were injured. Executives, including the chairman, were later convicted.

Step 2: Key decisions

Three decisions matter most. The first was to change the building from its original use to a department store during construction. A store needs open floors and escalator openings, so columns were reduced in size and slab openings cut. The second was to add a further floor, used for restaurants, with heavier floor finishes. The third was to place heavy air-conditioning equipment on the roof, which was later reported to have been moved across the roof, loading a structure that had no margin left. Each decision was made for commercial reasons by people who were not the structure's owner.

Step 3: Assumptions

The decision makers assumed the building could absorb the changes because it was already standing. That is the most dangerous assumption in construction: that a structure which holds today has spare capacity. The building was a flat-slab design, where slabs rest directly on columns without beams. In that system the critical point is where the slab meets the column. Thinner columns and heavier loads concentrate force exactly there, and the failure mode, called punching shear, is sudden. It gives little ductile warning of the kind a steel beam gives as it bends.

Say that out loud now.

Step 4: Incentives

Retail floor area earns rent and sales. Larger openings, more floor and more equipment all served revenue. The cost of strengthening, or of saying no, was immediate and visible. The cost of the risk was invisible until the day it arrived. When the people holding the revenue also hold the authority to approve structural change, the incentive bends the decision. Reports also describe an earlier contractor who refused to carry out the changes and was replaced. A professional who says no and is removed is a warning sign in itself.

Step 5: Warning signs ignored

Cracks appeared in the ceiling and slab in the period before the collapse, worsening on the final day. Engineers were reportedly called and indicated that the building was in danger. Senior management left the building, but the store was not closed and shoppers were not evacuated. A crack in a flat slab near a column is not a cosmetic issue. It is the structure announcing its failure mode.

Step 6: Point of no return

The physical point of no return came when the slab-to-column connections lost their remaining capacity. The human point of no return came hours earlier, when the decision was made to keep trading rather than evacuate. Up to that moment, nobody needed to die. After it, the structure decided.

Step 7: Root cause

The root cause was that the building's use, loads and layout were changed without the structure being re-engineered for them by someone with the authority and independence to refuse. The design was never re-checked as a whole. Each change was approved on its own merits, by people optimising revenue.

Translate it to a small project. A hypothetical owner adds a rooftop pool deck to a residential building after the structure is designed, because it will lift rents by a hypothetical 5 percent. The pool, water and deck add a load the roof was never designed for. If the change goes to the structural engineer of record before construction, it is a redesign costing perhaps a hypothetical 60,000 dollars. If it goes straight to the contractor, it is a gamble with the frame. The rent increase is real; so is the load.

The prevention rule

Rule 108: Never let a change of use, load or layout pass a stage gate, or reach site, until the structural engineer of record has re-checked the whole structure for it and confirmed in writing that it works.

Professional sign-off required: structural engineer of record, for any change to loads, openings or column sizes; architect of record, for any change of occupancy.

What a small developer should take from it

You will never run a department store of that size, so it is tempting to file Sampoong under someone else's scale. Do not. The pattern is ordinary. A tenant wants an opening widened. An operator wants equipment on the roof. A buyer wants a mezzanine. A contractor wants to swap a specified beam for one available sooner. Each request is reasonable alone, each saves or earns money, and each touches the structure.

The control does not need to be expensive. Keep one register. Every change that touches loads, openings, members or use goes on it with a date. Send the whole register, not the single change, to the structural engineer of record at each stage gate and before each change is built, and ask for a signed letter that the structure works with everything on the list. Pay for that letter. A few thousand dollars of engineering is the cheapest insurance on the project.

And decide, in writing and before you need it, who has authority to clear a building or stop work when a structural warning appears. On site that is usually the contractor's superintendent with the engineer; in an occupied building it is the owner or the property manager. If nobody owns that decision in advance, it will be made, as at Sampoong, by whoever is worried about the day's revenue.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is a series of small approved changes that nobody adds up. The control is a structural change register: every change that touches load, openings or members goes on it, and the engineer of record signs a cumulative check, not a change-by-change one.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner treats visible cracking as a maintenance item and calls a contractor. Cracks near columns, at beam ends or that grow over hours are a structural engineer's call, and the first decision is whether to clear the building.

Callback

In Week 99 you studied Champlain Towers South, where engineering warnings were treated as budget items. Sampoong is the same lesson faster. In both, the people who could pay for safety were told, and decided the money mattered more. Rule 99 and Rule 108 together say: a structural warning is a safety decision first.

Recap

Sampoong changed use during construction, lost column size, gained a floor and a heavy roof load, showed cracks, and was not evacuated. The root cause was structural change without a whole-building re-check by someone able to refuse. Rule 108 makes that re-check a condition of every change.

Next: Sage on The Money: what the design phase does to cost, value and yield on cost.
checklist: I keep a structural change register for every change to load, openings or members.
I require a cumulative, written re-check from the structural engineer of record for each change.
I never let a change of use reach site without an updated code analysis.
I treat cracking near columns or beam ends as a structural emergency.
I know who has the authority to clear the building, and it is written down.
I note any professional who refuses work and find out why before replacing them.
head: Field checklist
speak: Sampoong in Seoul collapsed on 29 June 1995 and killed more than 500 people. It was converted during construction to a department store. Columns were reduced, slab openings were cut, a floor was added and heavy equipment went on the roof. It was a flat-slab building, where the critical point is the slab at the column, and that fails suddenly in punching shear. Cracks grew for hours on the last day. Management left; the shoppers were not evacuated. The root cause was that use, loads and layout changed without someone independent re-checking the whole structure with the authority to refuse. So my rule is Rule 108: no change of use, load or layout passes a stage gate or reaches site until the structural engineer of record has re-checked the whole structure and confirmed in writing that it works. And a crack near a column is a call to an engineer and a decision about clearing the building, not a maintenance ticket.
terms: Change of use — altering what a building or space is used for, which can change its loads, occupancy and code requirements.
Flat slab — a concrete floor system where slabs rest directly on columns without beams.
Punching shear — a sudden failure where a column pushes through the slab around it.

hostile.q: The operator wants a rooftop amenity added and says the roof looks strong enough. Why are you delaying a change that lifts rent?
hostile.a: Because looks are not a load check. The change goes on the structural change register today and to the engineer of record for a whole-building check. If it works, we build it with a priced change order. If it needs strengthening, we price that and decide. I will not let a load reach the roof that the engineer has not signed for in writing.

rule: Rule 108: Never let a change of use, load or layout pass a stage gate, or reach site, until the structural engineer of record has re-checked the whole structure for it and confirmed in writing that it works.

title: Checkpoint: How Design Decisions Move Cost, NOI and Value
summary: Every design decision in the phase shows up in the pro forma as cost, net operating income or risk. This checkpoint lesson ties floor height, resilience, envelope and services to yield on cost, and shows how a cheap design can destroy value. Warrick's Wealth Ledger and a short thread on decision journals close it.
body:
Design is the pro forma drawn in three dimensions. A decision that saves first cost but raises operating cost, insurance or risk can lower value even as it lowers the budget.

Recall

Q. What is the last responsible moment?

A. The latest point at which a decision can be made without closing a better option or forcing rework.

Q. Why are elevators a long-lead design item?

A. Because the number, speed and size of cars fix the shaft, the machine space and the structure, and the equipment itself can take many months to deliver, so the decision must be made early.

Q. What is yield on cost?

A. Stabilised net operating income divided by total development cost, the return the building earns on what it cost to build.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, lenders and investors read the design through the pro forma. They do not ask whether the envelope is elegant. They ask what it costs, what it saves, and what can go wrong. This lesson gives you the translation from every design week into money.

Four channels from design to value

A design decision reaches value through four channels. First, capital cost, which raises or lowers total development cost. Second, operating cost, which raises or lowers net operating income (NOI), the income left after operating expenses and before debt. Third, revenue, through rentable area, quality and the rent the market will pay. Fourth, risk, through insurance premiums, downtime, repair and the exit cap rate a buyer applies.

Value at stabilisation is NOI divided by the capitalisation rate, or cap rate. So one dollar of permanent operating saving is worth roughly one divided by the cap rate in value. At a hypothetical 6 percent cap rate, a 10,000-dollar annual saving is worth about 166,000 dollars of value. That is why life-cycle cost matters: it is the bridge from engineering to price.

Worked example: the floor-to-floor decision

A hypothetical building has 100,000 square feet of gross area and a total development cost of 40,000,000 dollars. Stabilised NOI is 2,600,000 dollars, a yield on cost of 6.5 percent.

The team proposes cutting floor-to-floor height by 6 inches to save facade and structure. Saving, say 400,000 dollars. Total cost falls to 39,600,000 dollars. If nothing else changed, yield on cost rises to about 6.57 percent.

But the mechanical engineer reports that ducts no longer fit above the corridor ceilings, so units lose ceiling height and some ducts must run exposed. The leasing team estimates a 1 percent rent discount across the building. If gross rent is 4,000,000 dollars, that is 40,000 dollars a year less NOI. NOI falls to 2,560,000 dollars and yield on cost to about 6.46 percent, lower than where you started. At a 6 percent cap rate, the 40,000 dollars a year of lost income is about 667,000 dollars of lost value, against 400,000 dollars saved. The saving destroyed value.

Say that out loud now.

Worked example: paying for resilience

Now the other direction. Raising critical electrical equipment above the design flood level and adding flood barriers costs a hypothetical 300,000 dollars. The insurer quotes a premium reduction of 30,000 dollars a year and a lower deductible. The 30,000-dollar saving at a 6 percent cap rate is worth 500,000 dollars of value, before counting the avoided downtime. A buyer will also view the building as lower risk, which may show up as a slightly lower exit cap rate. Resilience that the market can see is not a cost; it is an investment with a measurable return. Resilience the market cannot see still protects your equity, but you should not count it in value unless an insurer or buyer will pay for it.

Where cheap design hides its cost

The phase showed five places. Envelope details that save first cost but leak, which become repair and vacancy. Mechanical systems sized without humidity control in a hot-humid climate, which become mould claims. Fire strategies that rely on a performance-based alternate, which carry permanent inspection obligations. Structures with no margin, which close off future changes of use. And services such as water storage and elevators sized for the minimum, which fail at peak demand and become complaints and turnover. Each looks like a saving in the budget and a loss in the operating statement.

Wealth Ledger

Warrick's point for your personal balance sheet: your equity in a project is the residual after the debt, so design decisions move your share of value far more than the project's. If value falls by 667,000 dollars on a project financed at 65 percent loan to value, the whole loss lands on equity. Hold design quality at the level that protects that residual, and never let a value-engineering list be approved by someone whose fee falls when the budget falls.

Worked example: the envelope over thirty years

A third comparison, because envelopes are where cheap design most often bites. Option A is a sealant-dependent facade costing a hypothetical 3,000,000 dollars, with resealing every 10 years at 300,000 dollars. Option B is a rainscreen facade with a drained cavity costing 3,400,000 dollars, needing only inspection and minor repair, say 40,000 dollars every 10 years.

Over 30 years, without discounting, Option A costs 3,000,000 plus three reseals of 900,000, about 3,900,000 dollars. Option B costs 3,400,000 plus 120,000, about 3,520,000 dollars. Discounting narrows the gap, because the reseals come later, but it does not reverse it in this example. And Option A carries the bigger risk: a missed reseal becomes water inside the wall, mould, tenant complaints and vacancy. A buyer's surveyor will notice the difference and price it into the offer.

The lesson for the pro forma is simple. Ask the cost consultant for first cost, the replacement and maintenance schedule, and the failure consequence for every major system choice. Put the annual equivalent into the operating budget, not a footnote.

Who should sign the trade-off

One more control. The person who proposes a saving should not be the person who approves it, and nobody whose fee rises or falls with the budget should be the final word on value. The cost consultant prices the four channels, the engineer of record confirms safety, and you decide, with the reasons written in the decision log. That separation costs nothing and stops most of the expensive mistakes in this lesson.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is value engineering judged on capital cost alone. The control is a rule that every proposed saving is priced in all four channels, capital, operating, revenue and risk, before approval, and that any saving touching the envelope, structure, fire or life safety needs the engineer of record's written consent.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner reads a lower budget as a better deal. Measure the deal by yield on cost and value, not by the size of the cost figure.

Decision journals, a monthly thread

Kema's thread this month is the decision journal. When you approve a design trade-off, write down the date, what you chose, what you expected it to cost and save, and what would prove you wrong. Review it at completion and again a year into operation.

Over a career, that journal becomes your own reference class. You will see which savings you were right about and which ones came back as repairs. Nobody else can give you that data about your own judgment.

Callback

In Week 10, Sage taught that value is NOI divided by the cap rate. This phase shows that the design is where most of that NOI is made permanent. A design choice is a cap-rate multiplier waiting to happen, in one direction or the other.

Recap

Design reaches value through capital cost, operating cost, revenue and risk. Price every saving in all four. A permanent operating change is worth about one over the cap rate in value. Cheap design often hides its cost in operations and risk.

Next: Ivo on The Rules: how the code basis, permits and alternates govern the whole design.
checklist: I price every design saving in capital cost, operating cost, revenue and risk.
I convert permanent operating savings to value using the cap rate.
I check whether an insurer or buyer will pay for a resilience upgrade before counting it.
I require written consent from the engineer of record for savings touching structure, envelope, fire or life safety.
I judge design changes by yield on cost and value, not by budget alone.
I record each design trade-off in my decision journal with what would prove me wrong.
head: Field checklist
speak: Design reaches value through four channels: capital cost, operating cost, revenue and risk. Value is net operating income divided by the cap rate, so a permanent saving of 10,000 dollars a year at a 6 percent cap rate is worth about 166,000 dollars. That is why a cheap design can destroy value. In my example, cutting floor height saved 400,000 dollars, but the lower ceilings cost 1 percent of rent, 40,000 dollars a year, worth about 667,000 dollars. The saving lost money. Going the other way, raising electrical gear above the flood level cost 300,000 dollars and saved 30,000 a year in premiums, worth about 500,000. So I price every saving in all four channels before I approve it, and anything that touches structure, envelope, fire or life safety needs the engineer of record's written consent. On a leveraged deal, every loss of value lands on my equity first.
terms: Net operating income (NOI) — the income a property earns after operating expenses and before debt service and tax.
Value engineering — reviewing a design to reduce cost while keeping its function, which can backfire if judged on first cost alone.
Exit cap rate — the capitalisation rate a buyer is expected to apply to NOI when the building is sold.

hostile.q: Your contractor has a value-engineering list worth 1,500,000 dollars. Why haven't you taken it?
hostile.a: I have taken the items that save money in all four channels. The rest are savings in capital cost that cost more in operations, revenue or risk. For each rejected item I can show you the operating or rent impact converted to value at our cap rate. On those items, taking the saving would lower the building's value by more than it lowers its cost.

title: Checkpoint: The Code Basis Is a Chain of Answers, and the Authority Holds the Last One
summary: This checkpoint lesson revisits how the building code governs design: adoption by a jurisdiction, occupancy, construction type, height and area, fire and egress, the referenced standards, special inspections and alternates. It explains who decides, what the permit actually approves, and where an owner gets caught.
body:
The building code is not one rule book. It is a chain of questions answered in order, each answer narrowing the next, and the final answer belongs to the authority having jurisdiction, not to your consultants.

Recall

Q. What are the four channels through which a design decision reaches value?

A. Capital cost, operating cost, revenue and risk.

Q. What does the American Society of Mechanical Engineers standard ASME A17.1 cover?

A. Safety requirements for elevators and escalators. Which edition applies depends on what the jurisdiction has adopted.

Q. In code terms, what is the difference between transient and residential occupancy?

A. Transient occupancy, such as a hotel, houses people for short stays who may not know the building, while residential occupancy houses people longer term. The code generally treats transient occupants as less familiar with exits, which can change requirements.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, every design week rested on the code, but the code is not self-executing. A jurisdiction adopts it, amends it, interprets it and enforces it. An owner who understands that chain can plan a permit. An owner who does not will be surprised by a plan review comment months into design.

Adoption: which code, which edition

In the United States the International Building Code (IBC), published by the International Code Council, is a model code. It has no legal force until a state or local government adopts it, often with local amendments, and often an edition or two behind the newest. The IBC then references other standards, for example ASCE 7 for loads, ACI 318 for structural concrete, the National Fire Protection Association (NFPA) standards for sprinklers and alarms, and ASME A17.1 for elevators. Those referenced standards are adopted with it, at the editions the code names.

The first question on any project is therefore: which code, which edition, with which amendments, does this jurisdiction enforce today? Your architect must write that answer at the top of the code analysis. If a project crosses a code-adoption date, ask which edition governs the permit application. Verify against the current adopted edition before relying on any provision.

The chain of answers

The code basis runs in a fixed order. Occupancy classification comes first: what the spaces are used for. Then construction type: what the building is made of and how fire-resistant its elements are. Then allowable height and area, which depend on both, and can increase with sprinklers and with frontage on open space. Then fire separations between occupancies, the fire protection systems the code triggers, and the means of egress: exits, travel distance, corridor ratings and accessibility.

Say that out loud now.

Worked example. A hypothetical building combines ground-floor retail with apartments above. The architect classifies each use, then chooses whether to treat them as separated occupancies, with rated fire separations between them, or as non-separated, where the whole building must meet the most restrictive requirements. Separation costs rated floors and walls; non-separation can cost height, area or more fire protection everywhere. Neither is right in general. The point is that it is a decision, made early, with a cost each way, and it belongs in the decision log.

What the permit approves, and what it does not

The building permit approves the construction documents as submitted for compliance with the code, as reviewed. It does not certify that the design is free of errors, that it meets your brief, or that it will perform. Plan review is a sample, not a guarantee. If the drawings are wrong and the reviewer misses it, the obligation to build to code generally remains with the owner and the designers. Professional responsibility sits with the licensed designers who sealed the drawings.

The code also requires special inspections for certain work, such as structural concrete, structural steel, soils and some fire-resistant construction, carried out by qualified inspectors usually engaged by the owner, not the contractor. The IBC places these in its chapter on special inspections and tests [unverified — confirm independently which items your adopted edition lists]. A statement of special inspections, prepared by the design professional, is typically submitted with the permit. The owner pays for the inspector, and must keep the inspector independent of the contractor.

Alternates and interpretations

When a design cannot meet a prescriptive requirement, the code allows an alternative material, design or method if the building official finds it at least equivalent in quality, strength, effectiveness, fire resistance, durability and safety [unverified — confirm independently the exact wording in your adopted edition]. This is how performance-based fire and smoke strategies are approved. The approval is discretionary and documented, and it may carry permanent conditions such as testing and maintenance.

Worked example. A hypothetical alternate saves 250,000 dollars of construction by replacing a rated corridor with enhanced sprinklers and detection. The approval requires annual testing at a hypothetical 6,000 dollars. Over 30 years, without discounting, that is 180,000 dollars, plus the risk that a future owner fails to test and loses the approval. The alternate still saves money, but it is not free, and it is an obligation that runs with the building.

Ratios and practice are not code

Many numbers in design are commercial practice rather than code: target floor-to-floor heights, efficiency ratios of rentable to gross area, elevator wait-time targets. They are useful, and negotiable, and you must not present them to an authority or lender as requirements.

Professional sign-off required: architect of record, for the code analysis; structural engineer, for the statement of special inspections for structure; fire protection engineer, for any alternate on fire and smoke.

When the code is unclear

Codes are written in general language and buildings are specific, so interpretation is constant. The building official has authority to interpret the code for the jurisdiction. The disciplined approach is to ask for interpretations early and in writing. A written determination, issued before design is fixed, is a record you can rely on; a verbal comment at a counter is not.

If you disagree with a determination, most jurisdictions provide an appeals process, often a board of appeals, with limits on what it can decide [unverified — confirm independently for your jurisdiction]. An appeal costs time. Usually the better route is to bring a design professional's written analysis to a meeting with the official and seek agreement, then record it. Treat interpretations as part of the code basis: list them in the code analysis, with dates, so the next reviewer, inspector or buyer can see why the building is the way it is.

Worked example. A hypothetical design depends on reading two mezzanine levels as part of the floor below, which keeps the building one storey lower for height limits. If the interpretation is confirmed in writing at pre-application, the design proceeds with confidence. If it is assumed and the plan reviewer disagrees at permit, the redesign may cost months. The letter costs a meeting.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is designing to the wrong code: the wrong edition, missing a local amendment, or misclassifying occupancy. The control is a written code analysis, agreed with the building department at a pre-application meeting, and updated at every stage gate.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner treats the issued permit as proof the design is right. The permit is the authority's review of what it saw. Your designers own the design, and you own the obligation to build it correctly.

Callback

In Week 32, Pax taught entitlements: zoning sets what you may build on the land. The building code sets how you must build it. A project needs both, and many developers learn the hard way that a zoning approval for a height says nothing about whether the code allows that construction type to reach it.

Recap

The code is adopted, amended and enforced locally, with referenced standards at named editions. The basis runs occupancy, construction type, height and area, separations, systems, egress. The permit approves what was reviewed, not that the design is right. Special inspections are the owner's, independent of the contractor. Alternates trade cost for permanent conditions.

Next: Quincy on The Numbers: reverse engineering a design budget from the value a building must achieve.
checklist: I know which code edition and local amendments govern my permit application.
My architect's written code analysis states occupancy, construction type, height, area and egress basis.
I hold a pre-application meeting with the building department to agree the code basis.
I engage special inspectors myself and keep them independent of the contractor.
I record every alternate approval and its permanent conditions.
I never present a commercial target as a code requirement.
head: Field checklist
speak: The building code is a model code until a jurisdiction adopts it, with its own amendments and often an older edition. It brings referenced standards with it, like ASCE 7 for loads and ACI 318 for concrete. The code basis is a chain answered in order: occupancy, construction type, allowable height and area, fire separations, systems, and egress. Each answer narrows the next. The permit approves what the reviewer saw; it does not certify the design is right, and the licensed designers own the design. Special inspections are paid for by the owner and must stay independent of the contractor. Alternates let you meet the intent another way, but they are discretionary and can carry permanent testing duties that run with the building. So my control is a written code analysis, agreed with the building department before design is far along, and updated at every stage gate.
terms: Model code — a code written by a private body, such as the International Building Code, that has no force until a government adopts it.
Special inspection — inspection of specified critical work by a qualified inspector, typically engaged by the owner, in addition to the building department's inspections.
Alternative method — a design or material not described in the prescriptive code, approved by the building official as equivalent.

hostile.q: The permit is issued. Why are you still paying for a code review and special inspections?
hostile.a: Because the permit is the authority's review of what it saw, not a guarantee. The obligation to build to code stays with us, and the special inspections are a code requirement the owner must fund and keep independent. If the reviewer missed something, a defect found after occupancy is our cost, our liability and a problem at sale. The review and inspections are cheaper than that.

title: Reverse Engineering a Design Budget from the Value the Building Must Achieve
summary: Start from the finished outcome, the value and yield a buyer and lender will accept, and work backward to the hard-cost budget, then to cost per square foot, then to what each design system can afford. This even-week lesson runs the calculation step by step with hypothetical round numbers.
body:
Most owners ask what the design will cost. The better question is what the design is allowed to cost, given what the finished building will be worth, and then make every discipline design to that number.

Recall

Q. What does the building permit approve?

A. The construction documents as submitted and reviewed for code compliance. It does not certify that the design is free of errors.

Q. What does a domestic water booster pump system do?

A. It raises water pressure where the street supply cannot reach the upper floors at an adequate pressure, usually with several pumps so one can fail or be serviced while the others run.

Q. What does design flood elevation mean?

A. The flood level a building must be designed for under the adopted code and floodplain rules, usually with freeboard, an added margin, above it.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, a design budget set by adding up what the consultants want will drift upward until the deal fails. A budget set by working back from value gives every consultant a ceiling, and makes trade-offs visible early, while they are cheap.

Step 1: Start from the outcome

A hypothetical apartment building will have stabilised net operating income (NOI) of 3,000,000 dollars a year. The lender and investors require a yield on cost of at least 6.5 percent, because the market cap rate is about 5.5 percent and they want a development spread of about 1 percentage point. These targets are commercial practice, not standards; they vary by market and cycle.

Maximum total development cost equals NOI divided by required yield on cost.

3,000,000 dollars divided by 0.065 equals about 46,150,000 dollars.

Check the value: 3,000,000 divided by 0.055 equals about 54,550,000 dollars. The margin over cost is about 8,400,000 dollars.

Step 2: Take out everything that is not hard cost

From 46,150,000 dollars, subtract:

  • Land: 6,000,000 dollars.
  • Soft costs, such as design, permits, legal, marketing and developer fee: assume 18 percent of hard cost.
  • Finance costs, such as interest during construction and loan fees: assume 3,000,000 dollars.
  • Owner's contingency: assume 5 percent of hard cost.

Let H be hard cost. Then 46,150,000 equals 6,000,000 plus 3,000,000 plus H plus 0.18 H plus 0.05 H.

So 37,150,000 equals 1.23 H.

H equals 37,150,000 divided by 1.23, about 30,200,000 dollars.

Say that out loud now.

Step 3: Convert to a rate

The building has 120,000 square feet of gross floor area. Hard cost per square foot equals 30,200,000 divided by 120,000, about 252 dollars per square foot.

Now compare that with what the market says this building type costs. If your cost consultant's benchmark for this quality and location is 270 dollars per square foot, you have an 18-dollar gap, about 2,160,000 dollars. You must close it before design starts, not after bids arrive.

Step 4: Split the rate among systems

Your cost consultant allocates the 252 dollars per square foot to major elements using typical shares for the building type, for example:

ElementShareDollars per square foot
Substructure and foundations8 percentabout 20
Superstructure20 percentabout 50
Envelope16 percentabout 40
Interiors and finishes18 percentabout 45
Mechanical, plumbing, fire protection20 percentabout 50
Electrical, elevators, specialties11 percentabout 28
Sitework and general conditions7 percentabout 18

These shares are illustrations, not norms. Each discipline now has a design-to-cost target. The envelope consultant knows the facade must come in near 40 dollars per square foot of floor, which, with a facade-to-floor ratio of 0.45, is about 89 dollars per square foot of wall.

Step 5: Close the gap the right way

Second worked example. To close the 2,160,000-dollar gap, the team has three kinds of lever. Efficiency: raising the ratio of rentable to gross area from 82 to 84 percent adds rentable area, which adds NOI. If rent is 30 dollars per rentable square foot a year net, 2 percent of 120,000 is 2,400 square feet, worth 72,000 dollars a year of NOI, which at 6.5 percent supports about 1,108,000 dollars more cost. Scope: simplifying the building's shape cuts facade area. Quality: lowering finish levels saves money directly, but check the rent impact, as in Sage's floor-height example.

Notice what you never touch to close the gap: structural margin, fire protection, flood resilience and the envelope's water control. Those are the savings that come back as failures.

Step 6: Test the backward budget

A backward budget is only as strong as its inputs, so stress them. Suppose the investors raise their required yield on cost from 6.5 to 7 percent because interest rates rose. Maximum total cost becomes 3,000,000 divided by 0.07, about 42,860,000 dollars. Repeat Step 2: 42,860,000 minus 9,000,000 equals 33,860,000, divided by 1.23, gives hard cost of about 27,530,000 dollars, or about 229 dollars per square foot. A half-point move in the investors' return requirement cut the design budget by about 23 dollars per square foot, roughly 9 percent.

Now try NOI. If rents come in 5 percent lower than planned, and operating costs stay the same, NOI may fall by more than 5 percent, because expenses do not fall with rent. Say NOI drops to 2,800,000 dollars. At 6.5 percent, maximum cost is about 43,080,000 dollars, and hard cost falls to about 27,700,000 dollars. These are the two numbers that move the design budget most, which is why the pro forma and the design must be revised together at every stage gate, not separately.

Write the sensitivities in a small table for the lender: base, rate up half a point, rent down 5 percent. It shows that you know how much room the design really has.

Reading the result back

When you present the backward budget, say it in the order a lender thinks. "The building earns 3,000,000 dollars of net operating income. Our investors need 6.5 percent on cost, so the whole project may cost about 46,150,000 dollars. After land, finance, soft costs and contingency, the construction budget is about 30,200,000 dollars, or 252 dollars a square foot. The market benchmark is 270, so we have a gap of about 2,160,000 dollars, and here is how we close it." Five sentences, every number traceable. If a listener can repeat it back, the budget is understood.

Keep the equation, the inputs and their sources on one page. When a cost consultant or investor challenges a number, you change that input and rerun the page in front of them, rather than defending a total nobody can trace.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is a design-to-cost target that the market rate cannot meet, which leads designers to cut quietly in the places nobody inspects. The control is to reconcile the backward budget with the cost consultant's benchmark at concept stage, and to change the deal, the program or the rent assumption openly if they do not meet.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner computes the hard-cost budget and then adds the contingency on top, double-counting it, or forgets that soft costs move with hard costs. Solve for hard cost with every percentage-based cost inside the equation, as in Step 2.

Callback

In Week 17, Sage taught reverse engineering a deal from public information: the implied land price and rent behind a sale. This is the same technique pointed at design. In both cases you start with what someone will pay and work back to what each input may cost.

Recap

Start from NOI and required yield on cost to get maximum total cost. Take out land, finance, and the percentage-based soft costs and contingency, solving for hard cost. Convert to a rate, compare with market benchmarks, split it into design-to-cost targets, and close any gap through efficiency, scope and quality, never through safety.

Next: Marco on The Room: a mock design review meeting at the final stage gate.
checklist: I compute maximum total development cost from NOI and required yield on cost.
I solve for hard cost with percentage-based soft costs and contingency inside the equation.
I compare the resulting rate with my cost consultant's benchmark at concept stage.
I give each discipline a written design-to-cost target.
I close gaps through efficiency, scope and quality, and I check rent impact.
I never close a budget gap by cutting structure, fire, flood resilience or envelope water control.
head: Field checklist
speak: I reverse engineer the design budget from value. NOI of 3,000,000 dollars at a required yield on cost of 6.5 percent supports a total cost of about 46,150,000. Take out land of 6,000,000 and finance costs of 3,000,000. Soft costs at 18 percent and contingency at 5 percent move with hard cost, so I solve: 37,150,000 equals 1.23 times hard cost, which gives about 30,200,000. Over 120,000 square feet that is about 252 dollars per square foot. If the market says 270, I have a 2,160,000-dollar gap, and I close it before design starts. I split the rate into targets for each system, so every consultant designs to a ceiling. I close gaps through efficiency, scope and finish quality, checking rent impact as I go. I never close a gap by cutting structural margin, fire protection, flood resilience or the envelope's water control, because those savings come back as failures.
terms: Design to cost — giving each design discipline a cost target derived from the project budget and requiring the design to meet it.
Efficiency ratio — rentable area divided by gross area, a measure of how much of the building earns rent.
Facade-to-floor ratio — external wall area divided by floor area, a driver of envelope cost.

hostile.q: Your cost consultant says the market rate is 270 dollars a foot and your budget allows 252. Isn't your deal already broken?
hostile.a: Not if I close the gap now, and I have a plan for most of it. Two points of efficiency adds about 1,100,000 dollars of supportable cost through rent. Simplifying the massing cuts facade area, and finish levels in back-of-house space come down. If those do not close the full gap at design development, I will change the deal or the program openly rather than let the designers cut structure, fire or envelope quietly.

title: Mock Meeting: The Final Design Stage Gate
summary: A full mock meeting at the final design stage gate, with the architect, structural engineer, fire protection engineer, cost consultant and the lender's monitor at the table. A late request to add a rooftop amenity and a cost overrun arrive in the same hour. Learn the lines to say, the lines never to say, and when to stay silent.
body:
The final design stage gate is the last cheap moment to say no. Run it as a decision meeting, not a presentation, and leave with every open item owned, dated and written down.

Recall

Q. In the reverse-engineered budget, what never gets cut to close a gap?

A. Structural margin, fire protection, flood resilience and the envelope's water control.

Q. What is the four control layers idea in envelope design?

A. A wall or roof must control water, air, vapour and heat, each with a continuous layer, and the layers must line up at every joint and penetration.

Q. What is a travel distance limit?

A. The maximum distance a person may have to walk from any point in a space to an exit, set by the code for each occupancy.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, this is the full mock meeting for the design checkpoint. In the room: the architect of record, the structural engineer of record, the fire protection engineer, your cost consultant and the lender's monitor, the independent engineer reviewing the design for the lender. You chair. The design is at the end of construction documents, ready for permit and pricing. Two problems arrive in the first hour.

Scene one: the late amenity

The architect opens: "The operator has asked for a rooftop deck with a hot tub. Marketing says it lifts rents. We can show it on the permit set by Friday."

The question behind the question: will you let a revenue idea skip the gate?

Say: "Thank you. It goes on the structural change register today. Before it goes on any drawing, I want the structural engineer's whole-building check, the fire engineer's view on roof occupancy and egress, and a price. We will decide when we have all three."

Turn to the structural engineer: "Can you tell me by next Wednesday whether the roof and the columns below it carry this, and what strengthening costs if not?"

Never say: "It's just a deck; the roof is designed for snow anyway." You do not know the roof's margin, and the hot tub's water is a concentrated load. That sentence is how Sampoong happened.

Then stop talking. Let the engineer name the date.

Say that out loud now.

Scene two: the overrun

The cost consultant reports: "The construction-document estimate is 1,800,000 dollars over the design-to-cost target. Mostly mechanical and envelope." The lender's monitor writes something down.

The question behind the question, from the monitor: does the owner have control of cost, or is the budget a hope?

Say: "Understood. Let us split it into three groups: scope growth since the last gate, pricing changes in the market, and estimating differences. Scope growth we reverse unless it is a code or safety item. For the rest, I want a value-engineering list priced in capital, operating, revenue and risk by next Friday, and I want the engineers of record to mark anything that touches structure, fire, flood or envelope water control as not available."

To the monitor: "You will have the reconciled estimate and our decision list before we issue for pricing."

Never say: "We'll find it in the bids." That tells the lender you are planning to be surprised.

A worked number to have ready. If the 1,800,000 dollars cannot be closed, how much does it cost the deal? On a hypothetical total cost of 46,000,000 dollars and NOI of 3,000,000 dollars, yield on cost falls from about 6.52 percent to about 6.28 percent. You should be able to say that calmly: "If we close none of it, yield on cost drops by about a quarter of a point. That is still above our floor, but it eats a third of our contingency equivalent, so we will close most of it."

Scene three: the fire engineer's flag

The fire protection engineer says quietly: "One thing. The mechanical drawings show a new duct route through the stair pressurisation shaft wall. Nobody issued it to me."

This is the most important sentence in the meeting, and it was said quietly. The question behind it: will the owner hear a coordination failure, or reward the person who raised it?

Say: "Thank you for catching that. That is exactly what this gate is for. Architect, please own that interface. I want the route resolved and issued to all disciplines before permit submission, and a check of every other penetration of a rated shaft."

Never say: "Can we deal with that in construction?" A penetration through a rated shaft is a fire strategy question, and it gets cheaper only on paper.

Closing the meeting

Read back every action, owner and date. "Structural check on the deck, Wednesday. Value-engineering list priced in four channels, Friday. Shaft penetration resolved and reissued before permit. The design is frozen except for those items. We meet again in ten days to decide."

Then ask the hardest question yourself, before the lender's monitor can: "Is there anything any of you is not comfortable signing for at this stage?" Wait through the silence. Count to five.

Holding your state

Two problems in an hour can feel like the project is slipping. It is not. It is the gate working. Breathe out slowly before you answer the overrun, keep your voice at the pace you used to open, and remember that the lender's monitor is reading your composure as much as the numbers.

Working with advisers, a monthly thread

The fire engineer's quiet flag is a lesson in managing advisers. The adviser who brings you bad news is the one protecting your money. If raising a problem ever costs someone standing in your meetings, the problems will stop being raised, and they will still be there.

Thank the person who found it, in front of the others, every time. Then give the problem an owner and a date.

Scene four: the monitor's question

Near the end, the lender's monitor asks: "Your flood report uses the effective flood map. Have you considered the preliminary map the agency released for comment?"

The question behind the question: is the design basis current, or will the lender inherit a building that sits below the next map's flood level?

If you know the answer, say it in one sentence. If you do not, say: "I do not know the answer to that today. Our civil engineer will compare the ground floor and critical equipment levels against the preliminary map and report to you in writing by next Friday, with the cost of raising anything that falls short."

Never guess. A confident wrong answer about a flood level is remembered for the life of the loan. "I don't know, and here is when you will know" is a strong answer in a room of engineers.

One last discipline: write the meeting note yourself, or have it written that day, and send it to everyone in the room by the next morning. The note is the record of what was decided, and the first version circulated is usually the one people remember.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is leaving the gate with open items that drift into permit or construction. The control is a written action list with owners and dates, a design freeze for everything else, and a follow-up decision meeting already in the calendar.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner runs the gate as a slide presentation and approves to keep momentum. A gate that never says no is a meeting, not a gate.

Callback

In Week 6, Kema taught the hostile-question method: acknowledge, bridge, answer, and the phrase "I'll confirm by Friday". Every answer in this meeting used it. You acknowledged each problem, bridged to a process, and gave a date.

Recap

Run the final stage gate as a decision meeting. Send late changes to the change register and the engineer of record before any drawing. Split overruns into scope, market and estimating, and protect safety items. Thank whoever finds a coordination failure. Leave with owners, dates and a freeze.

Next: Kema on the Checkpoint: the mock interview, the recorded explanation and your rules so far.
checklist: I chair the stage gate as a decision meeting with a written agenda.
I send every late change to the change register before any drawing.
I split overruns into scope growth, market pricing and estimating differences.
I have the yield-on-cost impact of an overrun ready to say aloud.
I thank anyone who raises a coordination failure, in front of the room.
I read back every action, owner and date before closing.
I ask whether anyone is uncomfortable signing, and wait through the silence.
head: Field checklist
speak: At the final design stage gate, I chair a decision meeting, not a presentation. A late rooftop amenity goes on the structural change register and to the engineer of record for a whole-building check, a fire view and a price before it appears on any drawing. I never say the roof can obviously take it. A cost overrun gets split into scope growth, market pricing and estimating differences. I reverse scope growth unless it is safety or code, and I ask for a value-engineering list priced in capital, operating, revenue and risk, with structure, fire, flood and envelope water control marked off limits. I know what the overrun does to yield on cost and I say it calmly. When the fire engineer quietly flags an unissued duct through a rated shaft, I thank them and assign an owner. I read back actions, owners and dates, then ask if anyone is uncomfortable signing, and I wait.
terms: Design freeze — a point after which the design may only change through the formal change procedure.
Lender's monitor — an independent engineer or cost consultant who reviews the design, budget and progress on the lender's behalf.
Coordination failure — a conflict between disciplines' designs, such as a duct through a rated wall, that no single consultant resolved.

hostile.q: You are 1,800,000 dollars over at construction documents. Why should I believe you will not be over again at bid?
hostile.a: Because I know where the 1,800,000 came from: scope growth, market pricing and estimating differences, and I am reversing the scope growth now. You will see the reconciled estimate and the priced decision list before we issue for pricing. I am also carrying the full overrun in my downside case: yield on cost falls by about a quarter of a point, which is still above our floor. I would rather show you that today than surprise you at bid.

role: Chief of staff and learning coach
title: Checkpoint: Designing the Building
summary: This is the checkpoint for the design phase. Answer six mock interview questions aloud, record a three-minute explanation of how a building is designed and governed on your phone, score it from 1 to 5 on accuracy, structure, composure and the hard question, and then read every rule so far aloud and restate it.
body:
You have learned the design phase when you can explain, out loud and without notes, how a building's big decisions lock, who signs each one, and what they do to cost and value. Today you test that and write down the score.

Recall

Q. In the mock stage gate, what should you do when the fire engineer quietly raises an unissued duct through a rated shaft?

A. Thank them in front of the room, assign the interface to one owner, and require it resolved and reissued to all disciplines before permit.

Q. What does Rule 108 say?

A. Never let a change of use, load or layout pass a stage gate, or reach site, until the structural engineer of record has re-checked the whole structure and confirmed in writing that it works.

Q. What is the outside view, or reference class forecasting?

A. Judging a project by how similar projects actually turned out, rather than only by the details of your own plan.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, this is Kema. The design phase is where you meet architects, engineers, code officials and the lender's monitor as the person who decides. They will test whether you understand the decisions you are signing. Reading these lessons builds recognition. Saying them aloud, under a little pressure, builds performance. This checkpoint measures performance and gives you a score to beat next time.

The mock interview

Imagine a senior credit officer and a design-savvy investor across the table. Read each question, answer aloud before reading the model answer, and be strict with yourself.

Question 1. In what order do the big design decisions lock, and why does it matter?

Answer: Use and occupancy, then construction type and height and area, then the flood and wind basis, then the structural grid and floor height, then stairs and shafts. Each answer constrains the next, so a late change to an early decision ripples through everything after it and costs many times more.

Question 2. What does the building permit prove?

Answer: That the authority reviewed the submitted documents for code compliance. It does not prove the design is error-free or meets my brief. The licensed designers own the design, and I own the duty to build it correctly.

Question 3. Your contractor offers a 400,000-dollar saving by lowering floor heights. How do you decide?

Answer: I price it in four channels: capital, operating, revenue and risk. If lower ceilings cost 1 percent of rent, say 40,000 dollars a year, at a 6 percent cap rate that is about 667,000 dollars of value, so I decline.

Question 4. How do you set a design budget?

Answer: I work backward from value: NOI over required yield on cost gives maximum total cost; I take out land and finance, solve for hard cost with soft costs and contingency inside the equation, convert to a rate, compare with the market, and give each discipline a design-to-cost target.

Question 5. What is an alternate method, and what does it cost after approval?

Answer: A design the building official accepts as equivalent to the prescriptive code. It can save capital, but it often carries permanent testing and maintenance conditions that run with the building, which I price and record.

Question 6. Why do you insist on a whole-building structural re-check for a small change?

Answer: Because structures fail at the sum of changes, not at any one. Sampoong in 1995 was converted during construction, lost column size, gained a floor and roof loads, and collapsed. Rule 108.

Say that out loud now.

The recorded explanation

Now the real test. Open the voice recorder on your phone and record a three-minute explanation of this phase, as if to a new equity partner who asks, "How do you stop the design from going wrong, and how do you know it is worth what it costs?" Use this order: the bottom line; the order in which decisions lock and the last responsible moment; one owner for every interface and stage gates with independent review; the code basis and what a permit does and does not prove; one worked number, such as the backward budget or the floor-height example; and one failure case with its rule. No notes. Do not restart if you stumble; stumbling is data.

Listen back once and score yourself from 1 to 5 on each of four measures:

  1. Accuracy. Were the definitions and numbers right? A 5 has no errors; a 3 has one material slip, such as saying the permit certifies the design.
  2. Structure. Did you lead with the bottom line and follow the order? A 5 could be written down as an outline.
  3. Composure. Was the pace steady, with pauses instead of filler words? A 5 sounds like someone who has chaired many design meetings.
  4. The hard question. Did you raise, unprompted, the risk a partner most fears, that a late change or a quiet saving undermines safety or value? A 5 raises it before the listener can.

Write the four scores and the date in your decision journal. An example of honest scoring: if you said "the engineers handle coordination" without naming who owns each interface, structure might still be a 4, but accuracy is a 3, because the phase's central idea is that interfaces fail when nobody owns them.

What to do with the scores

Any score of 3 or less points you back to a specific week. Accuracy errors on the code basis send you to Weeks 100 to 102. Errors on cost and value send you to Week 107 and this week's Day 3 and Day 5. Weak structure means you should rehearse the six-part outline twice and record again tomorrow. Composure improves fastest by recording often; the second recording is usually better than the first.

Here is a model outline, about three minutes when spoken. One: "We design in the order decisions become irreversible, and we make each one just before its last responsible moment." Two: "Use, construction type, flood level, structure and floor height, then shafts." Three: "Every interface has one named owner, and every stage ends with an independent review and a signed decision." Four: "The permit proves review, not correctness." Five: "Every saving is priced in four channels; cutting floor height to save 400,000 lost about 667,000 of value." Six: "Rule 108."

Rules I will not break

Below this lesson is the list of rules you have committed to so far, one from each failure case, now including Rule 108. Read each rule below aloud, then restate it in your own words. If you cannot restate a rule without looking, mark it and reread the lesson it came from this week.

A note on fairness to yourself. A first recording that scores 2s and 3s is normal and useful; it tells you exactly where to work. What matters is the second recording a week from now. Keep both files, and listen to the first one again just before you record the next.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk at a checkpoint is scoring what you meant instead of what you said. The recording does not know what you meant. Score the tape.

The beginner's mistake

Reading the model answers instead of recording. Reading feels like mastery and proves little. Hearing yourself explain a design under pressure is the rehearsal that makes the real meeting familiar.

Callback

In Week 84, the checkpoint for contracts and risk asked who pays when something goes wrong. This phase answers the earlier question: how to design so less goes wrong. Listen for whether your recording links them. A design with clear interface owners is easier to insure, contract and defend.

Recap

Answer the six questions aloud. Record three minutes on how a design is controlled and valued, score accuracy, structure, composure and the hard question from 1 to 5, and write the scores in your journal. Read every rule aloud and restate it.

checklist: RULES_SO_FAR
head: Rules I will not break
speak: This phase comes down to one idea: a building is designed in the order its decisions become irreversible. Use and occupancy lock first, then construction type and height, then the flood and wind basis, then the structural grid and floor height, then stairs and shafts. Each decision has a last responsible moment. Every interface between disciplines has one named owner, and every design stage ends with an independent review and a signed decision. The building permit proves the authority reviewed what it saw, not that the design is right. I price every saving in capital, operating cost, revenue and risk, because a cheap design can lower value. I set the design budget backward from value. And from Sampoong in 1995, Rule 108: no change of use, load or layout passes a stage gate or reaches site until the structural engineer of record has re-checked the whole structure in writing.
terms: Checkpoint — a scheduled test of whether a phase can be explained aloud under pressure, scored and recorded.
Decision journal — a dated written record of decisions, the reasons for them and the expected outcome, reviewed later against what happened.
Design-to-cost target — the cost ceiling given to each design discipline, derived from the value the building must achieve.

hostile.q: Your designers are licensed and insured. Why do you need to understand any of this?
hostile.a: Because each designer is responsible for their own discipline, and the failures happen between them and in the decisions only the owner makes: the use, the budget, the timing of changes and whether a saving is accepted. I do not design the building, but I decide what gets designed and when. Knowing the order of decisions and who signs each one is how I keep cost, value and safety under control.
